chapter_theme: Water-sport and the envoy: Tivittan's wives play against him in a garden pool, the play ends with drying, scenting and garlanding, and a Vidyadhara envoy flies down from the sky with a letter that begins to tell of a bride and her suitor.

cast.role: Tivittan, the dark-hued king, called by his colour
the kings' daughters who are his wives, who play in the water
attendants who open the pool's sluice
young attendants who tell the king the hour
the Vidyadhara who flies down with a letter
the woman of the queen's household who reads the letter

1675.reading: The king's wives, dark-haired, fill their syringes and pour streams like rain, fling garlands in play and shake the ear-ornaments from their shoulders, so turning themselves against their lord in sport.
1675.nuance: இறைவன்மேல் இனையர் ஆனார் says they became his foes in play; the poet uses the vocabulary of war for a bath, and the verses that follow keep it.
1675.event: The wives begin a water battle against the king, spraying him and throwing garlands.

1676.reading: The jets of scented water, aimed four ways from the syringes, fall on the wives like drops of fine rain, and the lord of the Nandaka sword, though the sport is only feigned, gives way before the women.
1676.nuance: Nandaka is the sword of Vishnu; calling Tivittan its lord keeps his godlike standing while he plays at losing. பொய்யே, 'only in pretence', is the poet's own word.
1676.event: Tivittan feigns defeat before the wives' water-jets.

1677.reading: As the lord's line of foot-guards breaks in the play, the water-toys and floating things are scattered, and, losing to the lily-wreathed women, he is said to have hidden like a crocodile in the pond's bent sluice.
1677.nuance: Line 2 (தரையாய்க் குறளுஞ் சிந்து மிதந்தன சில்ல சிந்தி) and the word ஓரையாய் in line 4 are obscure; the picture of a game lost and a hiding place is firm and the objects named are not.
1677.event: Tivittan, beaten at the water-play, hides in the pond's sluice like a crocodile.

1678.reading: The queens cry that they have beaten the hero and tell one another to pour the spray on him; while they play, their attendants open the lower sluice and the still water of the pool runs out with a rush.
1678.nuance: The words வென்றனம் வீரன் றன்னை வீக்குமின் are the queens' own cry; the draining of the pool is the poet's addition and shows the day's play ending.
1678.event: The queens declare victory over Tivittan, and attendants let the pool's water drain.

1679.reading: With garlands and cloth streaming water, the cane-sweet-voiced women loosen their dress, then draw their wet garments close and turn their shining faces aside, shy before the sea-hued lord.
1679.nuance: Shyness comes only after the play is over and the cloth clings; the poet puts modesty at the end of the sport and not at its start.
1679.event: The soaked queens gather their clinging garments and turn away shyly from Tivittan.

1680.reading: The queens tie up their jewelled girdles and loosened cloth, and with the gem-hued lord go down again into the golden pond, clinging to the floats at its side.
1680.nuance: Line 4 has dark bees and honey joining the hand-clasped play; the bees stand for black eyes or hair mingling with the flowers.
1680.event: Tivittan and the queens re-enter the pond with floats.

1681.reading: Women play in the water, now diving with swelling breasts, now clinging to a float with soft young-leaf hands, now ducking until their red carp-like eyes redden, and the poet says the water-play bewildered them.
1681.nuance: The verse is a series of three actions closed by மயங்கிற் றென்பவே, a hearsay close that keeps the poet at a distance from the scene.

1682.reading: Red saffron from their feet, evening-red powder and the dark collyrium dissolved from their long eyes mix together in the pool, so that the water seems to have been made red and dark at once.
1682.nuance: The water is described as the colour of what the women wash into it; nothing in the verse says it is stirred by the king.

1683.reading: The saffron paste of the women's breasts, the scented powder shaken from their hair and the sandal on the red-eyed lord's chest all mingle, and the great pool turns to mud.
1683.nuance: The turning of clear water into mud is meant as sign of the sport's abundance and not of spoiling; the poet makes no complaint.

1684.reading: The women strike the water with their broad hips and with their breasts under fine down, and bend their slim waists, so that the waves of the pool seem to be joining them.

1685.reading: As the women press into the water with garlands trembling on their young breasts, the lotuses that rose sank, and when the girls came up from their dive the new brightness of their faces showed to the lotuses.
1685.nuance: The conceit is that the lotuses show the girls' faces by contrast; the poet does not say they were outshone, only that the faces brought out something the flowers had not.

1686.reading: The clear waves tossed by the women with bangled hands rise, and as the tired women step towards the jewelled bank the water follows a little way up on their small feet and falls back again.

1687.reading: When the hours of the day had passed, the young attendants bow at his flower-anklets and tell him the time, and the king, with the vine-like painted-lipped women around him, goes to the day-time palace in the grove.
1687.event: Attendants tell Tivittan the time and he goes with his queens to the pleasure-house in the grove.

1688.reading: The wives dry the water from their jewel-coloured bodies, put fine cloth on their hips, and with smoke of aloe in a crow-beak vessel they perfume and dry one another's damp hair.
1688.nuance: It is not said whose body is dried; the grammar leaves open that the wives dry themselves or the lord. காகதுண்டம் (crow-beak) is a kind of aloe-wood.
1688.event: The queens dry and dress after the water-play and scent their hair with incense.

1689.reading: A garland is made of cool blue lilies, the dark-edged petals of the neythal, and the fragrant damanaka shoot, and it is received with joy.
1689.nuance: No one is named as maker or wearer; whose garland it is, and who rejoiced, is not said.
1689.event: A garland of lilies and damanaka is made and welcomed.

1690.reading: The wives rub the golden mountain-hued sandal of the southern hills into their skin and sprinkle lotus pollen over it, and their soft breasts become a feast for the king's eyes.
1690.nuance: விருந்து பட்டவே, 'became a feast', gives the breasts as what is offered to the lord; the poet's word fits a guest's treat and carries no blame.
1690.event: The queens paint their breasts with sandal and lotus pollen.

1691.reading: The young ones of beauty beyond counting come, bringing the cool bunches of kallaara lilies, the lily garlands they threw, and the shining lotuses, and embracing them.
1691.nuance: Whether இளையர் are young attendants or the young queens themselves is not clear; the verse names no giver and no receiver of the flowers.

1692.reading: The queens, with bunches of kallaara flower in their hands waved as fans, and lotus leaves held over them as umbrellas, appear like the lotus-seated goddess and her kind.

1693.reading: While the guardians of the quarters watch and the lord enjoys his sweet food, the girls stand around the destroyer of the great king, drinking him in with their dark eyes.
1693.nuance: மாவரசு அழித்தவன் recalls the earlier victory over the great king (the sarukkam's opening); the poet holds the war and the harem side by side in a single phrase.

1694.reading: As the king sits with the women, a Vidyadhara descends from the sky, enters the grove gate through the gatekeeper, and bows to the feet of the dark-hued lord.
1694.event: A Vidyadhara arrives from the sky, is let in by the gatekeeper, and bows to Tivittan.

1695.reading: When the visitor bows, the ruler of the wheel-ruled earth asks after the visitor's uncle and the welfare of the king whose feet he serves, and bids him rise, and, because the visitor bows as to Indra, bids him sit.
1695.nuance: Lines 1-3 are hard to construe: மாமனை நுவலி என்னை ... செவ்வியோ என்று can be read as Tivittan's question about the uncle, or the envoy's report of him; the reading follows the first.
1695.event: Tivittan asks after the sender and tells the bowing Vidyadhara to sit.

1696.reading: When they have settled, the envoy shows the letter, bowing to it; an attendant of the queen's household reads it aloud, and the king gives the envoy every ornament he wears except his crown.
1696.nuance: The gift comes before the sense of the message is told: the king rewards on seeing the letter, and the verse leaves the contents for the next verse. வாசித்து can mean 'reads' or 'discerns'; the reading takes it as read aloud.
1696.event: The envoy presents a letter, an attendant reads it out, and Tivittan gives the envoy all his ornaments but the crown.

1697.reading: The queens take the jewelled vessels from the visitor who has come through the cool moonlit sky, and, bidden to go on, he takes the letter again, and, told to say it again himself, bows to the feet of the king of the bright spear and speaks.
1697.nuance: The king's order இனியிது பெயர்த்து நீயே யுரை, 'now say this yourself, turned', makes the envoy answer in his own mouth what the paper holds; the verse does not say the paper's text was unfit.
1697.event: Tivittan has the envoy restate the message, and the envoy bows and begins.

1698.reading: The envoy begins: the king who rules the northern-ridge city of Surendrakanta has a daughter, broad-eyed and born of his queen, and the grandson of the fierce spear-bearing Veyyavan has asked for her in marriage.
1698.nuance: He names the bride by her father's city and her mother, and the suitor by his grandfather; who the suitor is, and what he wants of Tivittan, is for the verses after this chapter. The speaker is known from 1697.
1698.event: The envoy announces that a suitor has sought the daughter of the king of Surendrakanta.

links.note: 1675 opens the women's spray-war against the king; 1678 has the queens cry that they have beaten him and the pool run dry.
links.teaches: The water-play is told as a war from first volley to cry of victory, so the king's surrender is the planned end of the game.

links.note: 1694 has the Vidyadhara drop from the sky and bow; 1697 has the king make him tell the message in his own words.
links.teaches: The envoy's arrival is the start of an exchange which waits on the king's leave, shown in the order of events rather than said.

links.note: 1696 has the king give away all but his crown on seeing the letter; 1698 begins the message, which is a suitor's request for a bride.
links.teaches: The king pays for news before he knows what it asks, so the reward is for coming and not for what is said.

links.note: 1680 has the king and his wives clinging to a float in the pond; Akananuru 266 has the husband bathing with young women on a float, whose gossip the wife throws back at him.
links.teaches: The same float-play is a king's marital pleasure in the epic and a husband's scandal in the akam poem, so what makes it fair or shameful is who the partners are.

gains.a: The pond scene gains a measure of the play as a thing that, with other women, would be a wrong, which the epic never states.
gains.b: The wife's reproach gains a version of the same play with no reproach in it, showing that her anger is aimed at the partners and not the bath.

links.note: 1697 has the envoy take the letter, wait for the king's order and then bow and speak; Kural 687 says the best envoy knows the protocol, the moment and the place.
links.teaches: The epic shows an envoy in the sequence of bows, seating, gifts and leave to speak that the couplet names but does not show.

gains.a: The scene gains a standard by which the envoy's waiting and bowing read as skill and not only as courtesy.
gains.b: The couplet gains a concrete order of events in which an envoy shows he knows protocol and time.

source_issues: Verses 1675-1680, 1695-1698 were printed in eight half-lines and repaired into four lines by the build; read as four.
1677 line 2 is corrupt or hard (தரையாய்க் குறளுஞ் சிந்து மிதந்தன சில்ல சிந்தி) and line 4 ஓரையாய் is obscure.
1695 lines 1-3 are hard to construe and the speaker of the question is a reading.
1696 and 1697 leave unclear who reads the letter and who speaks.
